subject: RFI: VPC peering vs transit justification + egress audit requirements
messages:

Subject: RFI: VPC peering and egress controls for Redwood private deployment

Priya —

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. As part of our procurement RFI we need a short written justification for the network model Redwood proposes for a Private VPC deployment. Specifically:

1) Why VPC peering rather than a central transit gateway for our tenant VPCs?
2) How do you control egress from inference hosts to the public internet (NAT, proxy, egress firewall)?
3) What logs/retention and evidence can we get for quarterly audits (flow logs, connection metadata, TLS termination points)?

Can you provide a diagram (network pathways) and a one‑page justification we can include with the security questionnaire? Also flag any operational caveats we should be aware of (cross-region latency, peering limits, IP management).

—Sarah
Sarah Lewis
Lead InfoSec Analyst, Ellison Bank

From: Priya Natarajan <priya_natarajan@redwood.ai>
To: Sarah Lewis <sarah.lewis@ellisonbank.com>
Cc: markus_klein@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, monica_patel@redwood.ai

Subject: Re: RFI: VPC peering and egress controls for Redwood private deployment

Sarah —

Thanks for the clear list. Attached is a compact package we think will meet your auditors' needs: a diagram showing the proposed peering topology, an egress policy matrix, and our audit log retention statement. High level points:

- Peering rationale: For tenant‑isolated inference we recommend VPC peering when low-latency, dedicated L3 connectivity is required and the number of tenant VPCs is modest (<= 20 per account). Peering gives direct, single‑hop connectivity to inference subnets and avoids a centrally managed transit plane that can become a single operational dependency.

- Transit gateway tradeoffs: A transit gateway simplifies IP management and scales to many VPCs but introduces an additional network hop, potential throughput bottleneck, and a single point requiring RW ops access for routing changes. We recommend transit when customers expect 50+ VPCs, cross-account routing complexity, or policy enforcement at the cloud edge.

- Egress controls: By default, inference hosts are placed in private subnets with controlled NAT instances or managed NAT gateways per-tenant. Customers can opt for an egress proxy (TLS‑terminating edge) or an explicit egress firewall VPC with strict allowlists. For highly regulated customers we support an edge private link to a customer-managed bastion/proxy so that public internet egress is never initiated from Redwood-managed IPs.

- Auditability: We emit VPC flow logs, host-level connection metadata, and application-level request traces. Retention options: 90 days (default), 1 year, or custom. We can provide rolling extracts for quarterly audits via a signed S3 link or direct delivery to a customer log aggregator.

Attachments: vpc-peering-and-egress-diagram-v1.png (diagram), egress-policy-matrix.xlsx (matrix + examples), audit-log-retention-policy.pdf (policy).

I'll ping Markus and Karthik to confirm the exact phrasing for the diagram legend and the recommended default (peering vs transit) for your account size. Happy to do a short recorded explainer for auditors if that helps.

Best,

Priya Natarajan
Security & Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Priya / Sarah —

A couple of clarifications from the runtime/ops side that I asked to include in the final note:

- NAT vs Managed Proxy: For draft design, default is per-tenant NAT gateway for simplicity and minimal changes to customer routing. However, we strongly recommend a managed egress proxy for bank workloads because it centralizes TLS inspection, allowlisting, and outbound DLP integration. We can implement the proxy as a customer‑owned appliance reachable via VPC peering, or as a Redwood‑managed proxy when customers agree to our vetted egress IPs.

- IP exhaustion and peering limits: If Ellison expects rapid scaling across many VPCs, call out the 125‑peering per VPC limit (cloud provider dependent) and provide an IP plan. We recommend using small RFC1918 blocks per tenant and reserving a /22 per tenant for future growth.

- Cross-region considerations: Peering is regional; for multi‑region deployments we recommend a hybrid approach: peering within region, regional transit gateway for cross-region replication and failover (read throughput optimization).

I added three one‑line bullets to the diagram legend (see attached).

—Markus
Director, Runtime Operations
Redwood Inference

James / Sarah —

Quick answers to the three audit asks:

1) Sample export: Attached is a sanitized 30‑day VPC flow log CSV export (fields: srcAddr,dstAddr,srcPort,dstPort,protocol,bytes,packets,start,end,action) and a short README describing our sanitization steps. We can deliver the same export to your S3 or Splunk instance under an encrypted transfer.

2) TLS certs: If you opt for a Redwood‑managed egress proxy, TLS is terminated at the proxy; Redwood maintains cert lifecycle and provides cert CNs and OCSP responses. For highest assurance, we recommend a customer‑owned TLS termination (customer certs) on their proxy reachable via peering or private link — that ensures keys never leave Ellison. We support both patterns and document the key‑handoff process.

3) Retention SLA: Redwood default retention is 90 days. We contractually commit to 12 months on the Enterprise plan (addendum in our SOC2 package). For the RFI we can include a clause: "Redwood will retain VPC flow logs and connection metadata for 12 months and provide quarterly extracts within 5 business days upon request." We will also provide a signed manifest for each extract.

Next steps: I'll upload the sanitized log sample and a one‑page paragraph you can paste into the RFI doc. If the auditors want a short Zoom to walk through the export fields, Markus and I can join next week.

Regards,
Karthik Iyer
Head of Product Ops, Redwood Inference
